South Carolina property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment.

What the official sources say

  • Taxpayer must give the assessor written notice of objection within 90 days after the assessor mails the property tax assessment notice. (SC Code 12-60-2510(A)(3); source)
  • In years with no assessment notice, a taxpayer may appeal the fair market value, assessment ratio and assessment at any time, in writing to the assessor. (SC Code 12-60-2510(A)(4); source)
  • A written request to meet with the assessor within the 12-60-2510 time limits is a notice of objection; the taxpayer has 30 days after the conference to file a written protest with the assessor. (SC Code 12-60-2520; source)
  • Within 30 days after the county board's written decision, the taxpayer or assessor may request a contested case hearing before the Administrative Law Court. (SC Code 12-60-2540(A); source)
  • Legal residence (owner-occupied, up to 5 contiguous acres) is assessed at 4% of fair market value. (SC Code 12-43-220(c)(1); source)
  • Each county must appraise and equalize property once every fifth year. (SC Code 12-43-217(A); source)
  • Real property sold at a delinquent tax sale may be redeemed within 12 months by the defaulting taxpayer, a grantee, or a mortgage or judgment creditor. (SC Code 12-51-90(A); source)
  • Redemption interest on the bid: 3% in months 1-3, 6% in months 4-6, 9% in months 7-9, 12% in months 10-12, not exceeding the bid submitted for the forfeited land commission. (SC Code 12-51-90(B); source)

Who sets and collects property tax in South Carolina?

Property tax in South Carolina is run locally. The Department of Revenue says it is administered and collected by local governments with assistance from the department, and about two-thirds of county-levied property taxes support public education (SCDOR property tax page). Your county assessor values the house, the auditor and treasurer handle the bill, and school and city levies ride on the same notice.

That means rules in this guide come from the state code, while rates, office hours and payment options come from your county. Call the county treasurer before you finalize a sale date.

What assessment ratios does South Carolina use?

The state taxes a percentage of fair market value, and the percentage depends on use. The ratios below come from SC Code 12-43-220.

PropertyRatioSection
Owner-occupied legal residence, up to five contiguous acres4%12-43-220(c)
Other real property not otherwise provided for6%12-43-220(e)
Agricultural real property, qualifying individuals and partnerships4%12-43-220(d)(1)
Manufacturing and utility property10.5%12-43-220(a)(1)

A rental house or second home falls under the 6% line, so owner-occupants and investors see different bills on similar values.

How often are South Carolina properties reappraised?

Each county must appraise and equalize property once every fifth year (12-43-217). Valuation is to be complete by the end of December of the fourth year, with taxpayers notified of value or classification changes of $1,000 or more. New values are assessed in the fifth year.

A county may postpone putting revised values into effect by ordinance, for no more than one property tax year. If you plan to sell, find out which year your county is in. A reassessment year can move the bill your buyer inherits.

When is the bill due and what do late payments cost?

Taxes are due between September 30 and January 15 after assessment (SC Code 12-45-70). Penalties begin after the later of January 16 or 30 days after notices are mailed (12-45-180(A)).

If unpaid byPenalty added
The January deadline3%
Before the second day of the next FebruaryAdditional 7%
Before the seventeenth day of the next MarchAdditional 5%
Still unpaid in MarchTreasurer issues a tax execution, plus costs

A county may allow installment payments by ordinance. Taxpayers elect in writing between December 1 and January 15, and five installments of 16 2/3% fall on February 15, April 15, June 15, August 15 and October 15 (12-45-75). Taxes paid through escrow are excluded.

How do you appeal a South Carolina assessment?

Start with written notice of objection to the assessor within 90 days after the assessor mails the assessment notice (SC Code 12-60-2510). In years with no notice, an appeal may be made in writing at any time. One filed before the first penalty date applies to that tax year; one filed after applies to the next.

  1. Notice of objection to the assessor, or a written request to meet, within the 90 days.
  2. Conference with the assessor, scheduled within 30 days of the request or as soon after as practical (12-60-2520).
  3. Written protest within 30 days after the conference.
  4. Appeal to the county board of assessment appeals within 30 days after the assessor's response (12-60-2530).
  5. Contested case hearing before the Administrative Law Court within 30 days after the board's written decision (12-60-2540).

If an appeal is still open on December 31 of the tax year, the assessment is adjusted to 80% of the protested amount for payment purposes, with interest settled afterward (12-60-2550).

Who qualifies for the age 65 homestead exemption?

The homestead exemption removes the first $50,000 of fair market value of the dwelling for owners who are 65 by December 31, or who are disabled or legally blind, and have lived in the state at least a year (SC Code 12-37-250). It applies to county, municipal, school and special assessment real estate taxes. The application deadline is before July 16 of the tax year.

Our separate homestead page goes deeper. For sellers, the point is simple: a buyer who is not eligible will not carry the same exemption.

What happens to the 4% rate when you sell?

The 4% legal residence rate does not transfer automatically. The owner must apply before the first penalty date for the first year claimed, and when ownership changes the former owner must notify the assessor within six months while the new owner files a new application (12-43-220(c)(2)(vi)). Failing to notify or losing eligibility can bring a penalty of 100% of the tax paid plus interest at one-half of one percent per month (12-43-220(c)(2)(vii)(A)).

So a buyer who plans to live in the house should file promptly. A buyer who rents it out will be on the 6% ratio.

What if taxes go unpaid and the county sells the property?

Delinquent notices go out on April 1 or as soon after as practicable, and property is advertised once a week for three consecutive weeks (SC Code 12-51-40). The sale is a public auction, and the winning bidder pays in full that day.

The defaulting taxpayer, a grantee, or a mortgage or judgment creditor may redeem within twelve months of the sale (12-51-90). Interest on the bid is 3% in months one to three, 6% in months four to six, 9% in months seven to nine and 12% in months ten to twelve. Notice is mailed neither more than 45 days nor less than 20 days before the redemption period ends (12-51-120).

How is tax handled when a house sells mid-year?

If property changes hands after assessment, the new owner may apply before a tax execution sale, and the auditor estimates the share of tax owed on the portion acquired (12-45-140). Paying that share discharges the property from those taxes. Penalties must be waived when a house transferred mid-year, the notice went to the prior owner and the new owner got no timely notice (12-45-180(B)).

Closing agents normally settle the year's tax at the table. Tell your closing attorney about any unpaid prior-year bills so they show on the payoff list. A cash buyer can often close with back taxes owing, because the payoff comes out of proceeds.

What exemptions help sellers who build or flip houses?

South Carolina exempts 100% of the improvement value of newly constructed detached single-family homes offered for sale, for the period set out in 12-37-220(B)(51). The statute also exempts the first $10,000 of net depreciated value of business personal property for small businesses (12-37-220(B)(54)).

These exemptions are narrow and carry conditions. An investor who is rehabbing instead of building new should not assume the new-construction exemption applies. The county auditor can tell you.

Why does the county treasurer only collect certain bills?

County treasurers are prohibited from collecting any tax except what has first been entered on the tax duplicates of their county, or what the auditor has ordered (12-45-60). In practice, the bill your closing agent pulls will match the duplicate, and nothing outside it can be demanded at the table.

City or town taxes get the same relief as county taxes when a new owner pays a proportionate share (12-45-170). If land moves from one county to another by annexation, taxes are prorated between the two counties for that year (12-45-390).

What happens to the sale if the county takes the property?

On redemption, the officer cancels the sale in the tax sale book, and the purchaser is notified by mail to return the receipt for a refund of the price plus interest (12-51-100). After a tax deed is issued, the delinquent tax collector notifies the defaulting taxpayer and the owner of record of any excess due (12-51-60).

That excess is money left after taxes, penalties and costs. An owner who thinks a sale is coming should call the county delinquent tax office early. Selling before the auction avoids the twelve-month clock entirely.

More questions about South Carolina Property Tax Guide

When are South Carolina property taxes due?

Between September 30 and January 15 after assessment. Penalties start after the later of January 16 or 30 days after notices are mailed, beginning at 3% (SC Code 12-45-70, 12-45-180).

How long do I have to appeal my property assessment?

90 days after the assessor mails the assessment notice. In years without a notice you may appeal in writing at any time (12-60-2510).

Do I pay while an appeal is pending?

Yes. If the appeal is unresolved on December 31, the assessment is adjusted to 80% of the protested amount for payment, with a correction and interest afterward (12-60-2550).

Can I sell a house with back property taxes?

Yes, the unpaid tax and penalties are typically paid from sale proceeds at closing. Ask the county treasurer for a current payoff figure.

How long can a delinquent tax sale be redeemed?

Twelve months from the sale date, with interest on the bid that steps up from 3% to 12% (12-51-90).

South Carolina offers property tax relief for qualifying homeowners, and official sources explain the rules.

What the official sources say

  • First $50,000 of fair market value of the dwelling place is exempt from county, municipal, school and special assessment real estate taxes for owners who are 65+ (SC resident 1+ year), totally and permanently disabled, or legally blind. (SC Code 12-37-250(A)(1); source)
  • Failure to apply constitutes a waiver of the exemption for that year; application may be made in person, by mail with documentation, or online where the auditor has records. (SC Code 12-37-250; source)
  • 'Dwelling place' means the permanent home and legal residence of the applicant. (SC Code 12-37-250(A)(5); source)
  • Owner must hold fee simple title or a life estate; jointly owned by spouses qualifies if either meets the age/disability/blindness test. (SC Code 12-37-250(A)(1)-(2); source)

What is the South Carolina homestead exemption?

It exempts the first $50,000 of the fair market value of a dwelling place from county, municipal, school and special assessment real estate taxes for owners who are 65 or older, totally and permanently disabled, or legally blind. The rule is in S.C. Code 12-37-250.

It is a tax exemption on the home, not a creditor protection and not a freeze on the value. The South Carolina Department of Revenue describes it as a complete exemption from taxes on the first $50,000 of fair market value of your legal residence, and it is handled through the county auditor. You can read the statute on the Legislature's Chapter 37 page and the agency summary on the SCDOR exemptions page.

Who qualifies for the exemption?

An owner qualifies by age, disability or blindness, and by holding the right kind of title to the dwelling.

  • Age: a South Carolina resident for at least one year who turned 65 on or before December 31.
  • Disability: someone classified as totally and permanently disabled by a state or federal agency. A person who is not classified can ask the state Vocational Rehabilitation agency to evaluate the claim.
  • Blindness: a person who is legally blind as defined in Section 43-25-20.
  • Title: the owner needs complete fee simple title or a life estate. Life estates created by will count.

A home owned jointly by spouses qualifies when either spouse meets the test before January 1 of the tax year and the one-year residency requirement is met. The statute defines permanent and total disability as the inability to do substantial gainful work because of a medically determinable impairment lasting, or expected to last, at least 12 continuous months or ending in death.

How do you apply, and by when?

Apply in writing to the county auditor before July 16 of the tax year. An application filed after July 15 normally applies to the next year, with one exception for filings made before the first penalty date.

The statute allows three routes: in person at the auditor's office, by mail with proof of age, disability or blindness, or online where the auditor can check official records. Failing to apply waives the exemption for that year. The SCDOR says the individual form is PT-401I and that processing is currently 10 to 12 weeks, with MyDORWAY as the fastest filing method.

ItemWhat the sources say
Exempt amountFirst $50,000 of fair market value (12-37-250(A)(1))
Filing officeCounty auditor, with notice to the municipality
Written application cutoffBefore July 16 of the tax year
Individual formPT-401I (SCDOR)
Refund claimsWithin two years of the date taxes were paid (SCDOR)
Rollback periodCurrent year plus five preceding years (SCDOR)

The SCDOR page also notes that for tax year 2026 the state temporarily authorized an additional amount for certain recipients, and the county auditor decides whether it applies to you.

How is the homestead exemption different from the 4 percent legal residence rate?

They are two separate breaks. The 4 percent legal residence assessment lowers the taxable share of value for an owner-occupied home, while the homestead exemption removes the first $50,000 of value for qualifying seniors, disabled owners and blind owners.

The SCDOR states that the legal residence must be approved before a real estate exemption is granted, and the legal residence application goes through the county assessor. Under 12-43-220(c), the 4 percent ratio covers the home and up to five contiguous acres that the owner occupies as a legal residence. Other real property is assessed at 6 percent.

  • The legal residence application must be made before the first penalty date for the first tax year the owner claims it.
  • A residence rented for more than 72 days in a calendar year loses the 4 percent rate.
  • An owner who is found ineligible, or who fails to tell the assessor within six months of losing eligibility, can owe a penalty of 100 percent of the tax plus interest at one-half of one percent per month.

What happens to the exemption when you sell the house?

The exemption belongs to the owner's permanent home, so it stops with the sale and a buyer does not inherit it. The statute defines the dwelling place as the applicant's permanent home and legal residence.

A seller who moves in South Carolina can claim the exemption on the new residence, and a surviving spouse who moves must tell the auditor of the new address. A surviving spouse can also keep the exemption on the current home if they take complete fee simple title or a life estate within nine months of the death, and it continues while the spouse stays unmarried and uses it as a permanent home (12-37-250(D)).

The statute also says the exemption does not trigger a reassessment of the property. The five-year reappraisal cycle in 12-43-217 still runs on its own schedule, and a county may postpone implementing new values by one tax year.

How do taxes get handled at closing in South Carolina?

Real estate taxes are billed a year behind and are due between September 30 and January 15, so the closing statement usually splits the year between buyer and seller. The statute puts the penalty at 3 percent after January 15, with 7 percent more after February 2 and another 5 percent after March 17 (12-45-70 and 12-45-180).

If title changes after assessment, a new owner can ask the auditor to apportion the taxes and costs owed by the original owner before any tax-execution sale (12-45-140). When title transfers during the year and the notice went to the prior owner, the treasurer must waive penalties if the current owner never got a timely notice (12-45-180(B)).

The deed also carries a recording fee of $1.85 per $500 of value, made up of $1.30 for the state and $0.55 for the county (12-24-10). The grantor generally owes it (12-24-20). Confirm the numbers with your closing attorney and county office.

Can owners with other situations get relief?

Yes, several other exemptions exist, each with its own rules and form.

  • Disabled veterans: a dwelling with a lot not exceeding five acres.
  • Paraplegic or hemiplegic persons: a dwelling and lot up to one acre.
  • Medal of Honor or former prisoner of war recipients: a dwelling and lot up to one acre.
  • Disabled law enforcement officers and firefighters with service-connected disability: a dwelling with a lot not exceeding five acres.

These come from 12-37-220(B) and the SCDOR page. Ask your county auditor which fits before you list a home, since the right exemption can lower the carrying cost while you are waiting to sell.

Does the exemption cover mobile homes or shared ownership?

Yes in some cases. An owner of a mobile home on leased land may receive the exemption against personal property taxes under the same procedures, but cannot receive both the real and the personal property exemption in the same year (12-37-250(B)).

An owner-lessee who will own the home when the lease ends qualifies as though holding fee simple or a life estate. A part owner gets the owned percentage of the full exemption, with ownership under 5 percent treated as 5 percent, and the exemption cannot exceed the value of that interest (12-37-250(J)). Heirs who inherit a share of a parent's home should keep this in mind before a sale.

More questions about South Carolina Homestead Exemption

How much is the South Carolina homestead exemption?

The first $50,000 of the fair market value of your dwelling place is exempt from county, municipal, school and special assessment real estate taxes, under S.C. Code 12-37-250(A)(1).

What age do you have to be?

You must be 65 by December 31 and have lived in South Carolina for at least one year. Totally and permanently disabled and legally blind owners qualify without the age test.

When is the application deadline?

Written applications must be made before July 16 of the tax year. A later application generally takes effect the following year.

Does a buyer keep my homestead exemption?

No. The exemption applies to the applicant's permanent home and legal residence, so a buyer must qualify on their own and apply to the county auditor.

Does the exemption apply to a rental?

The 4 percent legal residence rate is lost if the home is rented more than 72 days in a calendar year, and the homestead exemption requires the home to be the owner's permanent residence.

This guide covers what official sources say about South Carolina estate and inheritance tax.

What the official sources say

  • Chapter 16, Title 12 imposes a tax equal to the federal credit on the taxable estate of residents (the federal credit no longer applies for post-2004 deaths per SCDOR). (SC Code Title 12, Ch. 16; source)
Selling in South Carolina?
We buy South Carolina houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Does South Carolina have an estate tax?

No. The South Carolina Department of Revenue states that South Carolina has no estate tax for decedents dying on or after January 1, 2005.

That means an heir who sells an inherited South Carolina house does not owe a state estate tax return before the sale can close. The page we opened addresses the estate tax only, so we do not make a statement about other state death taxes. Ask the Department of Revenue or a probate attorney if a specific question comes up.

The federal estate tax is a separate system. The IRS lists a filing threshold of $13,990,000 for deaths in 2025 and $15,000,000 for deaths in 2026, measured against the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption.

When does a federal estate tax return matter for a house?

Only a large estate must file a federal return, so most South Carolina families selling an inherited house will not. The IRS says simpler estates with cash, publicly traded securities, easily valued assets or jointly held property generally do not need to file.

A return can still be worth filing for a different reason. Since January 1, 2011, a decedent's estate may elect to transfer any unused exemption to a surviving spouse, and the election is made on a timely filed estate tax return.

South Carolina estate taxNone for deaths on or after January 1, 2005 (SCDOR)
Federal filing threshold, 2025 deaths$13,990,000 (IRS)
Federal filing threshold, 2026 deaths$15,000,000 (IRS)
Portability to a surviving spouseElected on a timely filed return, available since 2011 (IRS)
SC fiduciary income tax returnForm SC1041, due the 15th day of the fourth month after the tax year ends

What does an estate owe in South Carolina income tax after a sale?

The estate itself may owe income tax, and it files the SC1041 fiduciary return. A resident estate or trust must file if it must file a federal fiduciary return, has any South Carolina taxable income, or has a nonresident beneficiary.

The Department of Revenue lists other triggers too: gross income of $600 or more, or any trust with taxable income. Nonresident estates and trusts must file if they have income or gain from South Carolina sources.

  • The return and the payment are due by the 15th day of the fourth month after the tax year ends.
  • Filing extensions run up to five and a half months, but the Department says there is no extension of time to pay.
  • Estates and trusts must generally withhold on South Carolina income distributed to nonresident beneficiaries.
  • A liability of $15,000 or more per filing period must be filed and paid electronically.

A house sale may produce gain that flows through this return. Our South Carolina capital gains guide explains the 44 percent deduction that estates and trusts may use.

Who has the power to sell an inherited house in South Carolina?

The personal representative can sell, once appointed by the probate court. Under S.C. Code Section 62-3-701, the duties and powers of a personal representative commence upon appointment.

Section 62-3-715 allows a personal representative acting reasonably for interested persons to acquire or dispose of an asset, including land, at public or private sale, and to sell, mortgage or lease estate real property for cash or credit. Those powers are subject to a contrary will or court order and to Section 62-3-711(b).

Section 62-3-711(b) adds a limit: a personal representative may not sell real property except as authorized under Section 62-3-911 or the court procedures starting at Section 62-3-1301, unless the will authorizes it otherwise. Read the will first, because a sale power written into it can change what court steps are needed.

A buyer is protected. Under Section 62-3-910, a purchaser for value from a personal representative acting under a will's sale authority takes title free of the rights of heirs, devisees and other interested persons, and the same protection reaches a purchaser from a distributee holding a deed of distribution.

What probate deadlines affect the timing of a sale?

The creditor and contest periods set the clock, and several of them run for eight months or one year. A seller who knows these dates can plan the closing date.

  • Inventory: the personal representative must file an inventory and appraisement within ninety days of appointment, listing probate property at fair market value as of the date of death.
  • Creditor notice: the representative publishes notice once a week for three weeks in a county newspaper, asking creditors to present claims within eight months after first publication (Section 62-3-801).
  • Outside limit: claims that arose before death are barred unless presented within the earlier of one year after death or the notice period (Section 62-3-803).
  • Contesting informal probate: a contest may be filed within eight months of informal probate or one year after death, whichever is later (Section 62-3-108).

Claims secured by a lien on estate property are not cut off by those limits, so a mortgage or tax lien stays on the house until paid at closing. Section 62-3-909 also requires a distributee who received property improperly to return it, which is another reason to settle the estate with care before heirs split the proceeds.

Which closing costs follow an inherited house sale?

The deed recording fee is $1.85 per $500 of value, made up of $1.30 for the state and $0.55 for the county. The grantor is generally liable, and the buyer is liable second.

A deed from a personal representative is not on the exemption list we read, so plan to pay the fee unless an attorney finds an exception. Exemptions listed include corrective or quitclaim deeds that confirm title already vested with no consideration, and deeds in lieu of foreclosure to the mortgagee.

The real property tax bill is the other bill that follows the house. Sumter County's Treasurer, for example, says property taxes are paid one year in arrears, with notices each October and a January 15 payment date before penalties begin. Ask the county where the house sits for its schedule.

What problems do heirs run into with a South Carolina house?

Heirs often have to carry a house with no one living in it while probate runs. Taxes, insurance and utilities continue, and so do repair needs. Section 62-3-703 asks the personal representative to settle and distribute the estate as expeditiously as is consistent with the estate's best interests, so a slow, costly carry is something a representative has reason to avoid.

  • Several heirs who disagree on whether to keep or sell
  • Heirs living out of state who cannot visit the property
  • A house with deferred repairs the estate cannot fund
  • A tenant in a rental the decedent owned
  • Unpaid taxes or liens that must clear at closing

We buy houses as-is, including inherited properties, and we work with the personal representative's attorney on the paperwork. A written offer lets the heirs compare a cash sale with a listing that would first require repairs and cleanout.

Before you accept any offer, confirm that the personal representative has been appointed and has authority to sign. Expect the closing attorney to ask for proof of the representative's authority, and have the court's appointment papers ready.

More questions about South Carolina Estate and Inheritance Tax

Does South Carolina have an inheritance tax?

The Department of Revenue page we opened says South Carolina has no estate tax for deaths on or after January 1, 2005. It does not address any other state death tax, so confirm with the Department or a probate attorney.

How much can an estate be worth before the federal estate tax applies?

The IRS lists a filing threshold of $15,000,000 for deaths in 2026 and $13,990,000 for deaths in 2025.

Can an heir sell the house before probate ends?

Only the personal representative can sign for the estate, and the representative's powers start when the court appoints them. Section 62-3-711(b) restricts selling real property unless Section 62-3-911, the court procedures starting at Section 62-3-1301, or the will authorizes it.

How long do creditors have to make claims against an estate?

Notice is published once a week for three weeks and asks creditors to file within eight months of first publication. Claims arising before death are barred after one year from death, or sooner for creditors given notice.

Who files the estate's income tax return?

The fiduciary files Form SC1041 when the estate has South Carolina taxable income, gross income of $600 or more, or a nonresident beneficiary. The return and payment are due the 15th day of the fourth month after the tax year ends.

South Carolina evictions follow notice and court steps set by state law.

What the official sources say

  • Nonpayment: landlord may terminate if rent is unpaid five days after due, with written notice (can be in the lease) of nonpayment and intent to terminate. (SC Code 27-40-710(B); source)
  • Other breaches: written notice with termination not less than 14 days after receipt if not remedied. (SC Code 27-40-710(A); source)
  • Landlord may obtain evictions in magistrate's or circuit court without posting bond. (SC Code 27-40-710(C); source)
  • Evicted tenant's property placed on a public street is removed after 48 hours (excluding weekends/holidays); eviction notice must inform the tenant. (SC Code 27-40-710(D); source)
  • Week-to-week tenancy terminable on 7 days written notice; month-to-month on 30 days. (SC Code 27-40-770(a)-(b); source)
  • Month-to-month tenancy can be terminated by either party with 30 days' written notice. (SC Code 27-40-770(b); source)
  • Holdover tenants after lease end may be sued for possession; willful holdover can yield up to three months' rent or twice actual damages plus fees. (SC Code 27-40-770(c); source)

How does an eviction work in South Carolina?

A South Carolina landlord ends a tenancy with written notice, then asks a magistrate for a rule to show cause, and only a court-issued writ lets the tenant be removed. The landlord cannot change locks or shut off water to force the issue.

The two statutes that matter are Chapter 40 of Title 27 (the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act) and Chapter 37 of Title 27 (ejectment of tenants). The first says when a lease can be ended. The second sets the court steps. If you own a rented house and are thinking of selling it, you need to know where a tenant sits on that path, because it shapes what a buyer will pay for and when the keys can change hands.

Read the primary text at the South Carolina Legislature's Chapter 40 page and the Chapter 37 page.

What notice comes before a South Carolina eviction case?

The notice depends on the reason: five days for unpaid rent, fourteen days for most other lease breaches, and thirty or seven days to end a periodic tenancy. Each must be written.

SituationNotice or periodStatute
Rent unpaidFive days from the due date, with written notice of nonpayment and intent to end27-40-710(B)
Other lease breach not fixedTermination no sooner than 14 days after the tenant receives the notice27-40-710(A)
Week-to-week tenancyAt least 7 days written notice27-40-770(a)
Month-to-month tenancyAt least 30 days written notice27-40-770(b)
Tenant response to rule to show cause10 days after service27-37-20

The lease can carry the nonpayment warning itself. The statute even supplies the sentence a lease must contain about the five-day window, so a landlord should check that wording before relying on it.

What happens in magistrate court?

The landlord applies to the magistrate, who issues a rule telling the tenant to leave or appear and explain why not within ten days of service. If the tenant does nothing, a warrant of ejectment follows.

Service is where many South Carolina cases slow down. The statute lets the rule be served like a summons. If the home looks abandoned for 15 days or more, the rule may be fixed to the most visible part of the premises. After two failed attempts at least 48 hours apart, and at times at least eight hours apart, it may be posted and mailed through the clerk, and mailed service counts as complete ten days after mailing (27-37-30).

If the tenant appears and contests, the magistrate hears the matter like other civil cases, and either side may ask for a jury. Many landlords build a few weeks of slack into any closing date for this reason.

  • Rent keeps accruing at the old rate while the tenant stays, and taking rent does not give up the right to eject (27-37-150).
  • A judgment for the landlord leads to a writ of ejectment within five days (27-37-100).
  • A judgment for the tenant lets the tenant stay until the tenancy ends by agreement or law, or rent goes unpaid (27-37-110).

Who physically removes a tenant, and how fast?

A constable or deputy sheriff carries out the writ, and the occupants get 24 hours to leave voluntarily after it is presented. Only a deputy sheriff, not a constable, may force entry, and then only by the least destructive means (27-37-160).

The officer may delay removal for an ill or elderly tenant. When a tenant's belongings are set out on a public street, they are removed after 48 hours, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and holidays, and the eviction notice must tell the tenant so (27-40-710(D)).

An appeal is possible, but it does not stop the ejectment unless the tenant posts an appeal bond, and the appeal is dismissed if that bond is not filed within five days after service of the notice of appeal (27-37-120 and 27-37-130). A landlord can bring the action in magistrate's or circuit court without posting a bond (27-40-710(C)).

What can a landlord not do in South Carolina?

A landlord may not recover possession by cutting off essential services or any other self-help, except where the tenant has abandoned, surrendered or the tenancy has properly ended (27-40-760).

Several other rules protect tenants during a sale or an eviction:

  • Entry needs 24 hours notice at reasonable times, with emergencies excepted (27-40-530). That matters for showings and inspections.
  • Retaliation is barred. A tenant who wants to raise it as a defense to a rule to vacate must notify the landlord in writing within ten days of service, and a retaliating landlord can owe up to three months rent or treble damages (27-40-910).
  • Unexplained absence for 15 days after a rent default can be treated as abandonment, and left property valued at $500 or less may be disposed of under the conditions in 27-40-730.

A willful holdover after a lease ends can cost the tenant up to three months periodic rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater, plus fees (27-40-770(c)).

How does an eviction affect selling a rented house in South Carolina?

A pending case does not stop you from selling, but it changes the timeline and the type of buyer. Most financed buyers want a vacant house or a clean lease, which is why many owners with a tenant in default look at an as-is cash sale.

Think through these points before you list or sign a contract:

  • If a tenant has a valid lease, the deposit duties travel with the sale. A seller who conveys in good faith is relieved of later liability after written notice to the tenant, but stays responsible for the deposit unless it is transferred and the tenant is told (27-40-410 and 27-40-450).
  • Owner or agent contact details must be kept current and bind a successor owner (27-40-420(b)). Give the buyer that information in writing.
  • A buyer who does not want the tenant can only take the house vacant if the tenancy has ended lawfully. Do not promise a delivery date that depends on a court calendar you do not control.

When a tenant is current and the lease runs for months, selling subject to the lease may be the simpler route. When the tenant is in default or holding over, owners often prefer to sell the house with the tenant issue priced in.

What should a landlord check on a South Carolina property before selling?

Start with the lease, the rent ledger and the deposit record, then confirm your property tax status with the county.

Rented houses are not treated like owner homes for tax purposes. The 4 percent legal residence ratio does not apply to a residence rented for more than 72 days in a calendar year, and a property found ineligible can face a 100 percent penalty on the tax plus interest of one-half of one percent per month (12-43-220(c)). Other real property is assessed at 6 percent, so a rental can carry a heavier bill than the owner's own home would.

Property taxes are payable between September 30 and January 15. Penalties of 3 percent, then 7 percent more after February 2 and 5 percent more after March 17 follow (12-45-70 and 12-45-180). Ask the county auditor and treasurer for the current year's figures before a closing.

Where can a landlord or tenant get official help?

The best starting points are the county magistrate's office, which accepts the filings, and the primary statutes themselves.

Court clerks cannot give legal advice, so a landlord with a complicated case, a tenant claiming retaliation or a holdover dispute should speak with a South Carolina attorney. If you want to compare notes on how a sale could work around a tenant situation, our team can walk through it with you at no obligation, and you can read the statute text in full first.

More questions about South Carolina Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does a South Carolina eviction take?

There is no fixed total, because it depends on service and whether the tenant contests. The statutory pieces are a five-day or fourteen-day notice, a ten-day window after the rule is served, a writ within five days of a landlord win, and 24 hours to leave once the officer presents the writ.

Can a landlord lock a tenant out in South Carolina?

No. Section 27-40-760 bars recovering possession by self-help or by willfully cutting essential services, except for abandonment, surrender or proper termination.

How much notice ends a month-to-month lease?

Either side must give at least thirty days of written notice before the termination date under 27-40-770(b). A week-to-week tenancy needs at least seven days.

Can I sell a house while a tenant is being evicted?

Yes, nothing in the statutes bars a sale during a case. The buyer takes the property subject to the court process, and the deposit rules in 27-40-410 and 27-40-450 still apply to what is owed the tenant.

What happens to a tenant's belongings after an eviction?

Property placed on a public street is removed after 48 hours, not counting weekends and holidays. Abandoned property valued at $500 or less may be disposed of under 27-40-730 once its conditions are met.

A South Carolina deed is recorded with the county office named in the sources below.

What the official sources say

  • A corrective or quitclaim deed used to confirm title already vested in the grantee, with no consideration, is exempt from the deed recording fee. (SC Code 12-24-40(12); source)
  • Quitclaim deeds must meet the same recording requirements: signed and acknowledged before two witnesses or proved by subscribing witness affidavit. (SC Code 30-5-30; source)
  • If consideration is paid, the exemption does not apply; an affidavit stating the exemption reason is filed. (SC Code 12-24-40(12), 12-24-70(A)(2); source)
  • In counties other than the 25 listed counties (including Charleston, Greenville, Richland, Horry), the clerk of court performs the register of deeds duties; the listed counties have a register of deeds. (SC Code 30-5-10(A); source)
  • Before recording, a deed must be proved by a subscribing witness affidavit or acknowledged by the grantor in the presence of two witnesses before an officer competent to administer oaths. (SC Code 30-5-30; source)
  • The register of deeds records instruments in the order presented, once execution is proved. (SC Code Title 30, Ch. 5; source)

What does a quitclaim deed do in South Carolina?

A quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest the signer holds, and South Carolina treats it like other deeds for signing and recording. The deed must be proved or acknowledged before it can be recorded (SC Code 30-5-30), and the statute exempts quitclaim and non-warranty deeds from the derivation clause rule (30-5-35).

People use them to add a spouse, clear a name after divorce or move a house into a trust. Sellers sometimes ask whether one can substitute for a regular sale deed. It can transfer title, but a buyer's title company will look hard at it.

How must a South Carolina quitclaim deed be signed?

The deed must be proved or acknowledged in one of the ways allowed by 30-5-30, and the form in 27-7-10 contemplates two or more credible witnesses. The options in 30-5-30 are:

  • An affidavit from a subscribing witness
  • Compliance with the Uniform Recognition of Acknowledgments Act, or a signer's affidavit that the signature is theirs
  • The grantor's acknowledgment before an officer, witnessed by two witnesses

A warranty clause is not required, and the form may carry other clauses the parties consider proper (27-7-20). A seal is not required if the attestation shows the parties meant the instrument to be sealed (27-7-30).

Does a quitclaim deed avoid the deed recording fee?

Only in a narrow case. A corrective or quitclaim deed that confirms title already vested in the grantee, with no consideration paid or to be paid, is exempt from the fee (SC Code 12-24-40(12)). If money changes hands, the exemption does not fit.

The ordinary fee is $1.85 for each $500 of value or fraction (12-24-10). The clerk or register must require an affidavit of value, and for an exempt deed the affidavit must state the reason for the exemption (12-24-70(A)(2)). Willfully filing a false affidavit is a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine up to $1,000, up to a year in prison, or both (12-24-70(C)).

Which transfers are exempt from the fee?

The exemption list in 12-24-40 is long, and a few items come up in family and title situations:

TransferExemption number
Realty valued at $100 or less(1)
Transfers where no gain or loss is recognized under IRC Section 1041(4)
Partition with no consideration beyond the interests exchanged(5)
Family partnership to partner, or family trust to beneficiary, where the only consideration is a reduced interest(9)
Corrective or quitclaim deeds confirming title already vested, with no consideration(12)
Deed in lieu of foreclosure or foreclosure deed to the mortgagee(13)

A transfer between spouses incident to divorce often falls under item 4, but the facts matter. Ask the register of deeds or clerk, or a South Carolina attorney.

Who owes the fee, the grantor or the grantee?

The grantor is liable by default, jointly and severally if there are several, and the grantee is secondarily liable (12-24-20). The grantee is the liable party for master-in-equity deeds and for deeds from the federal government, a state or its subdivisions.

If the proper fee is not paid, the person liable can face a penalty of $50 to $500 per failure, and a clerk who fails to collect faces the same range (12-24-120). The Department of Revenue may waive or reduce either penalty.

Does a quitclaim deed handle joint tenancy and survivorship?

Survivorship in South Carolina depends on specific wording. A deed naming grantees followed by the words "as joint tenants with rights of survivorship, and not as tenants in common" creates a joint tenancy (27-7-40(a)). After a joint tenant dies, the survivor may file a certified death certificate with the register of deeds, and the filing is conclusive that the tenant is deceased (27-7-40(b)).

Divorce severs a husband-and-wife joint tenancy and leaves a tenancy in common without survivorship. If a quitclaim is meant to fix a title after a death or divorce, check which of these applies before you sign.

When does a quitclaim work for a house you plan to sell?

It works best for cleaning up who is on title before a sale, and less well as the sale deed itself. Common uses before a sale:

  • An heir who is not the personal representative releases an interest
  • An ex-spouse signs off after divorce
  • A co-owner transfers a share to the person selling

Title companies look at the whole chain, so a quitclaim in the chain may prompt questions. When an estate is involved, a deed of distribution from the personal representative is the usual instrument instead (62-3-907). Our probate page covers that.

Cash Home Buyers buys houses as-is, including ones with messy title. Send us what you have and we will tell you honestly whether the title needs work first.

Where do you file a quitclaim deed?

File it with the register of deeds, or the clerk of court in counties not listed in 30-5-10(A), in the county where the land sits. Deeds executed after July 1, 1976 need the grantee's mailing address (30-5-35). The register records instruments in order lodged and within thirty days of lodgment (30-5-90). See our recording page for the full list of steps.

What should you check before signing a quitclaim deed?

Treat a quitclaim as final, since the deed gives away your interest as soon as it is delivered and recorded. Use this checklist:

  • Confirm whether any money is changing hands, which decides whether the fee exemption applies
  • Get the signing witnessed by two people or arrange a subscribing witness affidavit (30-5-30)
  • Include the grantee's mailing address (30-5-35)
  • Prepare the affidavit stating the exemption reason if you claim one (12-24-70(A)(2))
  • Check for a mortgage, which a deed does not pay off

For a transfer into a trust or from a trust to its beneficiary, items 8 and 9 on the exemption list can matter. Moving property into a corporation, partnership or trust in exchange for an ownership interest, with no other consideration, is exempt, but transfers back out to the stockholder, partner or beneficiary are generally taxable (12-24-40(8)).

What other transfers does the fee statute address?

A few exemptions cover transfers that look like quitclaims but are different. Individual cemetery grave spaces sold by a licensed cemetery company are exempt (12-24-40(6)). So are contracts for the sale of timber to be cut (12-24-40(7)). Transfers to the federal government or to a state, its agencies and departments or political subdivisions, including school districts, are exempt (12-24-40(2)).

For a house, the more relevant cases are corrective deeds. If a legal description in an earlier deed was wrong, a corrective deed confirming title already vested falls under item 12 when no consideration is paid.

What does a quitclaim cost if the fee does apply?

If the exemption does not fit, the fee is the same $1.85 per $500 of value or fraction as any other deed (12-24-10), split $1.30 state and $0.55 county (12-24-90). A deed with $50,000 of consideration covers 100 units, so the statutory fee is $185. The liable party is the grantor by default (12-24-20), so the person giving up the interest may owe it.

More questions about South Carolina Quitclaim Deed

Is a quitclaim deed valid in South Carolina?

Yes, if it is signed and proved or acknowledged as 30-5-30 requires and then recorded. It conveys the grantor's interest without needing a warranty clause (27-7-20).

Do I pay a recording fee on a quitclaim deed?

Not if it merely confirms title already vested in the grantee with no consideration (12-24-40(12)). You still file an affidavit stating the exemption reason.

Does a quitclaim deed remove someone from a mortgage?

The statutes reviewed here say nothing on that point. Talk to your lender, since the deed and the loan are separate.

Can I use a quitclaim deed to sell my house?

You can record one, but buyers and title companies generally want to see the full chain of title. Ask a closing attorney which deed fits your sale.

Who pays if the fee applies?

The grantor by default, with the grantee secondarily liable (12-24-20).

South Carolina probate runs through the courts named in the sources below.

What the official sources say

  • Small estate affidavit: 30 days after death, successor may collect personal property by affidavit if the entire probate estate, less liens and encumbrances, does not exceed $45,000. (SC Code 62-3-1201(a); source)
  • The affidavit must state no PR appointment is pending, be countersigned by the probate judge, and be filed in the probate court of the decedent's domicile county. (SC Code 62-3-1201(a)(3),(5),(6); source)
  • Section 62-3-1201 governs collection of personal property; the extracted text does not authorize conveying real property by affidavit. (SC Code 62-3-1201; source)
  • A personal representative distributes real property by deed of distribution, which is evidence of the distributee's title. (SC Code 62-3-907; source)
  • Estates under summary administration may be closed by the PR's verified statement; PR appointment terminates one year after death if no unresolved claims are pending. (SC Code 62-3-1204; source)

When does a South Carolina estate need probate?

A will in South Carolina has to be validated by an order of informal probate or an adjudication of probate before it can prove a transfer of property or name a personal representative (SC Code 62-3-102). The main exception is the small estate affidavit, covered below. If a house sits in the decedent's name alone, the family usually needs a court-appointed personal representative before anyone can sign a deed.

There is also an outer limit. No informal, formal testacy or appointment proceeding may start more than ten years after the death, with a short list of exceptions (62-3-108). After that, intestacy is treated as incontestable if nothing was filed.

Who is allowed to act as personal representative?

South Carolina ranks who gets first call on the appointment, and the person named in the will comes first. Under 62-3-203 the order runs like this:

  1. The person with priority under a probated will, including a nominee named in it
  2. A surviving spouse who is also a devisee
  3. Other devisees
  4. A surviving spouse
  5. Other heirs
  6. A creditor, starting 45 days after death, if the creditor follows 62-3-804(1)(b)
  7. The South Carolina Department of Revenue or a suitable person the court picks, starting four months after death

Anyone under eighteen is disqualified. Siblings who disagree about who should serve are a common reason a house sits unsold for months, so settle that early.

What is the difference between informal and formal probate?

Informal probate starts with a verified application to the court; formal testacy is a litigated proceeding started by a summons and petition. The informal application must state the applicant's interest, the decedent's name, date of death, age and domicile, and the names and addresses of the spouse, children, heirs and devisees (62-3-301). It must also say the ten-year limit has not run.

Formal testacy exists to decide whether a valid will was left (62-3-401). While one is pending, the court may not act on informal probate or appointment applications. A contest of an informally probated will may be brought within eight months of informal probate or one year of death, whichever is later (62-3-108(A)(2)(c)). A buyer or title company will care about that window.

What deadlines apply after the personal representative is appointed?

Several clocks start at appointment, and a few start at death. Here are the ones in the probate article:

StepDeadlineSection
Notice of appointment to heirs and deviseesWithin 30 days of appointment62-3-705
Inventory and appraisementWithin 90 days of appointment62-3-704(b), 62-3-706(A)
Creditor claims after published noticeEight months after first publication62-3-801(a)
Outer limit for claims arising before deathOne year after death62-3-803(a)
Pay allowed claims before closingNo later than 14 months after death, absent an extension62-3-807(a)

These clocks decide when a family can safely distribute proceeds, which is a separate question from when the house can be sold.

Can a personal representative sell the house?

Yes, the statute lets a personal representative acquire or dispose of an asset, including land, for cash or on credit, at public or private sale (62-3-715). That power begins on appointment (62-3-701), so a sale contract signed before the court issues letters is on shaky ground.

At closing, the title company will want to see the letters, and a South Carolina deed from the estate is typically signed by the personal representative. Once the estate distributes real property instead of selling it, the personal representative must execute a deed of distribution to evidence the distributee's title (62-3-907(A)). Heirs who inherit and then want out can sell afterward, but that adds a recording step.

Bond can matter too. Bond may be waived by affidavit when the estate's gross value is under twenty thousand dollars (62-3-603(B)(1)), and an interested person or creditor with a claim over five thousand dollars may demand one (62-3-605). Ask the probate court how it handles bond in your county.

What does the $45,000 small estate rule cover?

South Carolina lets a successor collect personal property by affidavit when the whole probate estate, less liens and encumbrances, is worth no more than $45,000 (62-3-1201(a)). Real estate is the catch, and the section governs collection of personal property, so a house usually needs a personal representative anyway.

  • At least 30 days must have passed since death.
  • No application or petition for a personal representative may be pending or granted anywhere.
  • The probate judge of the decedent's county of domicile must approve and countersign the affidavit.
  • The affidavit is filed in that county's probate court.

A related summary route lets a personal representative close an estate not over $45,000 by sworn statement (62-3-1203, 62-3-1204), and the appointment ends one year after death if no claims or proceedings are pending.

How are creditors paid when the estate is short?

When assets run short, South Carolina pays claims in a set order (62-3-805). That matters if the house must be sold to cover debts.

  • Costs of administration, including attorney's fees and reasonable funeral expenses
  • Debts and taxes with preference under federal law
  • Reasonable medical, hospital and personal care costs of the last illness
  • Debts and taxes with preference under South Carolina law
  • All other claims

The personal representative must publish the creditor notice once a week for three successive weeks in a county newspaper (62-3-801(a)). A claim not presented in time is barred.

What is it like to sell an inherited house in South Carolina?

Most inherited-house sales in South Carolina slow down at the same few points: getting letters issued, finding the original will, agreeing among heirs, and clearing back property tax or liens. South Carolina has 46 counties, so local habits and timing vary. Call the probate court in the county where the decedent lived before you plan around a date.

Cash Home Buyers works with personal representatives and heirs who want to sell the house as-is. We can talk before appointment, but a closing needs authority to sign. Bring the death certificate, the will if there is one, and any court paperwork you already have.

What does a personal representative owe the heirs?

A personal representative is a fiduciary who must settle and distribute the estate under the will and the Code, as expeditiously as is consistent with the estate's best interests (62-3-703(a)). That duty applies to a house just as it does to bank accounts. Delay that costs the estate money, such as months of carrying costs on a vacant property, is the kind of thing heirs can question.

The personal representative also has the same standing to sue and be sued as the decedent had before death, except for proceedings that do not survive death (62-3-703(c)). The first person issued general letters has exclusive authority until that appointment ends or is modified (62-3-702). Acts that benefited the estate before appointment can relate back, and the personal representative may ratify acts others did for the estate (62-3-701).

Is there a faster path when one heir inherits everything?

Yes, a narrower one. If the appointed personal representative is the sole devisee or sole heir, that person may distribute the estate immediately after publishing the creditor notice and then file a closing statement (62-3-1203(b)). The closing statement is a verified document stating the estate was fully administered and distributed, and that a copy went to distributees and known unpaid creditors (62-3-1204(a)).

Under 62-3-301(a)(7) the court may also probate a will without appointing a personal representative. Whether that helps with a house sale depends on the title company, so ask before you list or sign anything.

What documents do you need to gather first?

Most delays come from missing paperwork. Start with this list:

  • A certified death certificate
  • The original will, if one exists, since the application must say whether the original is with the court or attached (62-3-402(a))
  • Names and addresses of the spouse, children, heirs and devisees, with ages for minors (62-3-301)
  • The current deed and a recent property tax bill
  • Mortgage statements and any lien notices

If the original will is lost, the petition must state its contents and say it is lost, destroyed or otherwise unavailable (62-3-402(a)).

More questions about South Carolina Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Do I need probate to sell a house in South Carolina?

Usually yes, if the house is titled only in the decedent's name. The will must be validated under 62-3-102, and a personal representative then has power to sell land under 62-3-715. Confirm your facts with the probate court.

How long does South Carolina probate take?

There is no single timeline. The statute sets deadlines such as 30 days for notice to heirs, 90 days for the inventory, and eight months for creditor claims after publication. Allowed claims should be paid by 14 months after death unless extended.

Can heirs sell the house without a personal representative?

Generally not. A deed from the estate needs someone with authority. The small estate affidavit in 62-3-1201 collects personal property and does not by itself authorize a deed to land.

What is a deed of distribution?

It is the deed a personal representative signs to pass real property to a distributee, and it serves as evidence of that person's title (62-3-907(A)).

Can someone contest the will after informal probate?

Yes. A contest may be started within eight months of informal probate or one year of death, whichever is later (62-3-108(A)(2)(c)).

This guide covers what official sources say about South Carolina tax on a house sale.

What the official sources say

  • SC allows individuals, estates and trusts a deduction equal to 44% of net capital gain recognized in SC. (SC Code 12-6-1150(A); source)
  • Net capital gain is defined by IRC Section 1222 and related sections. (SC Code 12-6-1150(B)(2); source)
  • H. 4216 (signed March 30, 2026): 1.99% rate on income under $30,000 and 5.21% minus $966 for $30,000 and above, effective tax year 2026. (Information about H. 4216 | SCDOR; source)
  • The top rate may be reduced further if the Board of Economic Advisors projects revenue growth of 5% or more, determined by Feb 15 annually. (Information about H. 4216 | SCDOR; source)
Selling in South Carolina?

Get My Cash Offer →

Does South Carolina tax capital gains when you sell a house?

Yes. South Carolina has no separate capital gains tax, but a taxable gain from a house sale is included in your South Carolina income and taxed at the regular income tax rates, after a 44 percent deduction.

Under S.C. Code Section 12-6-1150, individuals, estates and trusts may deduct 44 percent of the net capital gain recognized in the state during the year. Net capital gain takes its meaning from federal Internal Revenue Code Section 1222 and related sections.

In plain terms, the state starts with the same gain you report to the IRS, then lets you subtract 44 percent of it. Only the remaining 56 percent adds to your South Carolina taxable income.

What are the South Carolina income tax rates on that gain?

For tax years beginning after 2025, Section 12-6-510 sets a 1.99 percent rate on taxable income under $30,000 and, for $30,000 or more, 5.21 percent of the amount minus $966. The statute also ties later top-rate reductions, starting with tax year 2027, to state revenue projections.

Here is an illustration with made-up numbers. Suppose a South Carolina owner has a $100,000 net capital gain that is not covered by the federal home sale exclusion. The 44 percent deduction removes $44,000, so $56,000 is added to taxable income.

If that person had no other income, the $56,000 would fall in the upper bracket, and the formula gives 5.21 percent of $56,000 ($2,917.60) minus $966, or about $1,952. Real returns include wages, deductions and exemptions, so use this only to see how the formula works.

South Carolina itemWhat the statute says
Capital gain deduction44% of net capital gain recognized in South Carolina (12-6-1150)
Rate on income under $30,0001.99% (12-6-510, tax years after 2025)
Rate on income of $30,000 or more5.21% of the amount, minus $966
Net capital gain definitionInternal Revenue Code Section 1222 and related sections
Partnership and S corporation gainsCount as South Carolina income

Does the federal home sale exclusion carry over to South Carolina?

The South Carolina deduction starts from the federal net capital gain, so gain you exclude on your federal return is not part of the gain being taxed. The IRS lets you exclude up to $250,000 of gain from the sale of your main home, or up to $500,000 on a joint return.

You must have owned the home for at least 24 months and used it as your residence for at least 24 months within the five years before the sale. The two periods do not have to fall at the same time. You generally cannot claim the exclusion if you excluded gain on another home sale during the two years before this one.

If you receive a Form 1099-S, the IRS says you must report the sale even when the gain is fully excludable. For limits and exceptions to the two-year rule, the IRS points to Publication 523, Selling Your Home.

  • Primary residence for 2 of the last 5 years: the exclusion may apply
  • Rental or investment house: the gain is generally taxable
  • Inherited house: ask a tax professional about basis before you sell

How do federal capital gains rates affect a South Carolina seller?

The federal tax on a long-term gain is separate from, and added to, the South Carolina tax. A gain is long-term if you held the property more than one year, and net short-term gains are taxed as ordinary income.

The IRS table for tax years beginning in 2025 puts the 0 percent rate on taxable income up to $48,350 for a single filer and $96,700 for joint filers. The 15 percent rate runs up to $533,400 for single filers and $600,050 for joint filers, and 20 percent applies above that. The page we opened does not give 2026 thresholds, so check the current year before you plan.

The IRS also notes that people with significant investment income may owe the net investment income tax. A South Carolina investor who sells a rental may therefore face federal capital gains tax, the net investment income tax and the state tax in one year.

What happens if you live outside South Carolina when the house sells?

A buyer of South Carolina real estate from a nonresident seller must withhold tax at closing, under S.C. Code Section 12-8-580. The rate is the maximum individual rate applied to the gain for a nonresident individual, partnership, trust or estate, and five percent of the gain for a nonresident corporation or other entity.

If the seller gives the buyer an affidavit stating the amount of gain, withholding is figured on the gain. Without an affidavit, the same rates apply to the full amount realized, and the buyer withholds all of the net proceeds if the required amount is larger.

  • Gain on a principal residence that is excluded under the federal exclusion is outside the withholding rule.
  • The buyer must remit the withholding by the 15th day of the month after the sale month.
  • The buyer is liable for the amount, while lenders, agents and closing attorneys are not liable for collecting it but must remit what they actually withhold.
  • A seller can file an amended nonresident withholding statement to claim a refund of excess withholding.

An heir living in another state who sells an inherited South Carolina house is a nonresident seller for these purposes if the estate's decedent lived outside the state at death. Ask the closing attorney to prepare the affidavit early.

Which closing costs are separate from income tax?

The deed recording fee is a transfer cost, not an income tax, and it is $1.85 for each $500 of the property's value. That breaks into $1.30 for the state and $0.55 for the county per $500, and the grantor, meaning the seller, is generally liable for it.

Some deeds are exempt, including deeds in lieu of foreclosure to the mortgagee, deeds on foreclosure to the mortgagee, and corrective or quitclaim deeds that confirm title already vested with no payment. A deed for a master-in-equity sale puts the liability on the buyer instead.

Property tax is also settled at closing. Ask your county treasurer for the payoff figure before you set a closing date. In Sumter County, for example, the Treasurer says real property taxes are paid one year in arrears.

How do estates and trusts handle a gain on a house in South Carolina?

An estate or trust that sells a house can use the same 44 percent deduction, but only for income taxed to the estate, the trust or its individual beneficiaries. The deduction does not apply to income passed through to a beneficiary that is not an individual.

If you inherited a house, the gain depends on your basis, which is the value used to measure profit. The IRS page we opened sends readers to Publication 551 for the rules on inherited property, so we do not state a basis rule here.

Whether an inherited sale produces any taxable gain depends on facts we cannot see. A CPA can confirm the basis before you sign a contract.

What should you gather before talking to a tax professional?

Collect the numbers that set your gain before you list or accept an offer. A professional can only help if the figures are in hand.

  • The purchase closing statement and the date you bought
  • Receipts for improvements, such as a roof or an addition
  • The dates you lived in the house, if you moved out
  • Any depreciation you claimed if the house was a rental
  • The estimated sale price and selling costs

If you are selling a house that needs work, an as-is cash sale can shorten the time between the contract and the closing statement. Selling costs, the sale date and the net proceeds still affect your return, so keep every document.

More questions about South Carolina Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Does South Carolina have a capital gains tax?

South Carolina does not have a separate capital gains tax. Capital gains are taxed as part of South Carolina income, after a deduction of 44 percent of net capital gain under Section 12-6-1150.

What is the South Carolina income tax rate for 2026?

For tax years after 2025, the statute sets 1.99 percent on taxable income under $30,000 and 5.21 percent of the amount minus $966 at $30,000 or more. Later reductions starting in 2027 depend on state revenue projections.

Can I avoid tax on selling my main house in South Carolina?

Often you can avoid much of it. The IRS excludes up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 for joint filers, if you owned and lived in the home at least 24 months in the five years before the sale. Gain above the exclusion is still taxable.

Is there withholding if I live out of state?

Yes. A buyer from a nonresident seller must withhold under Section 12-8-580, at the maximum individual rate on the gain if you give an affidavit, or on the full amount realized if you do not. Gain excluded as a principal residence is outside the rule.

Who pays the South Carolina deed recording fee?

The seller, as grantor, is generally liable for the fee of $1.85 per $500 of value, and the buyer is secondarily liable. A master-in-equity deed shifts it to the buyer.

Deeds are recorded with the county office named in the sources below.

What the official sources say

  • In counties other than the 25 listed counties (including Charleston, Greenville, Richland, Horry), the clerk of court performs the register of deeds duties; the listed counties have a register of deeds. (SC Code 30-5-10(A); source)
  • Before recording, a deed must be proved by a subscribing witness affidavit or acknowledged by the grantor in the presence of two witnesses before an officer competent to administer oaths. (SC Code 30-5-30; source)
  • The register of deeds records instruments in the order presented, once execution is proved. (SC Code Title 30, Ch. 5; source)
  • The deed recording fee ($1.85 per $500) is collected before recording, with an affidavit of value. (SC Code 12-24-10, 12-24-70; source)
Selling in South Carolina?
We buy South Carolina houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Where do you record a deed in South Carolina?

You record it with the register of deeds, or with the clerk of court in counties that are not listed in SC Code 30-5-10(A). In those unlisted counties the clerk performs the register's duties with the same powers. Berkeley and Dorchester registers serve four-year terms.

South Carolina has 46 counties, so which office you need depends on where the land lies. Charleston, Greenville, Richland and Horry are among the counties with a register of deeds.

What must happen before a deed can be recorded?

The deed has to be proved or acknowledged first, and 30-5-30 allows three routes. Pick the one your closing attorney uses.

  • An affidavit from a subscribing witness
  • Compliance with the Uniform Recognition of Acknowledgments Act, or a signer's affidavit that the signature is theirs
  • The grantor's acknowledgment before an officer, witnessed by two witnesses

Deeds and mortgages executed after July 1, 1976 must include a derivation clause and the grantee's mailing address, and a clerk may not record one lacking the derivation clause unless the information was unavailable (30-5-35). Quitclaim and non-warranty deeds are exempt from the clause. Leaving something out does not by itself affect validity or record notice (30-5-35(c)).

How much does it cost to record a South Carolina deed?

The deed recording fee is $1.85 for each $500, or fractional part of $500, of the property's value (SC Code 12-24-10). It splits into a state share and a county share.

Part of the feePer $500
State$1.30
County$0.55
Total$1.85

On a deed valued at $200,000 that is 400 units of $500, so the statutory fee is $740. The state share is credited $0.10 to the Heritage Land Trust Fund, $0.20 to the South Carolina Housing Trust Fund and $1.00 to the general fund (12-24-90). The county share goes to the county general fund. The register may also charge separate filing fees, so ask the office for a current schedule.

What is the affidavit of value?

The clerk or register must require an affidavit showing the realty's value, signed by a responsible person connected with the transaction who states that connection (12-24-70(A)(1)). The clerk may waive it at discretion. Bring the closing statement figure.

For an exempt deed, value is not required, but the affidavit must state why the deed is exempt (12-24-70(A)(2)). A willfully false affidavit is a misdemeanor with a fine up to $1,000, up to one year in prison, or both (12-24-70(C)).

Which deeds are exempt from the fee?

12-24-40 lists fifteen exemptions. The ones sellers meet most often are listed here:

  • Realty valued at $100 or less
  • Transfers to the federal government, a state or its political subdivisions, including school districts
  • Transfers where no gain or loss is recognized under IRC Section 1041
  • Corrective or quitclaim deeds confirming title already vested, with no consideration
  • Deeds in lieu of foreclosure or deeds under foreclosure proceedings to the mortgagee
  • Transfers from an agent to the principal whose funds bought the realty, with a notarized document establishing the relationship

Treat any other transfer as taxable until the register says otherwise.

How quickly is a deed recorded and what do you get back?

The register records writings in the order they are lodged, and each must be recorded within thirty days of lodgment, with the recording bearing the lodgment date (30-5-90). The register or deputy endorses a certificate showing the time, book and page. No fee is charged for that certificate (30-5-200).

Certified copies are issued on application, with fees paid in advance if required (30-5-20). Order one after closing for your files.

Who is responsible if the fee is not collected?

The grantor is liable for the fee, and the grantee is secondarily liable (12-24-20). For master-in-equity deeds and deeds from the federal government, a state or its political subdivisions, the grantee is liable instead. A person who fails to pay can face a $50 to $500 penalty per failure, and a clerk who fails to collect faces the same range (12-24-120).

What should you bring to record a deed?

Bring the original signed deed, the proof or acknowledgment, the affidavit of value or exemption, the grantee's mailing address and payment for the fee. Estate deeds add one more item: a deed of distribution is how a personal representative passes real property to a distributee (62-3-907(A)), so bring the letters too.

A joint tenant's survivor files a certified death certificate with the register of deeds (27-7-40(b)).

Sellers working with Cash Home Buyers do not need to organize any of this alone. The closing attorney or title company usually records the deed, and we can walk you through it.

What if the deed is lodged in the wrong county?

South Carolina has a provision for transferring a recording to the correct county (30-5-100). Check the county before you lodge anything, because a recording in the wrong place delays the sale record and can hold up your buyer's title policy.

The county is the one where the land sits. A house near a county line is worth confirming against the tax bill.

Does the deed need a plat or a land use plan?

A land development or land use plan is not required before a deed for undeveloped land, though a local entity may still require a plat when the deed is recorded (30-5-30(D)). For a lot split or a deed of part of a parcel, call the planning office in the county or city before you head to the register.

An instrument is also not denied record because the probating officer left out a service serial number (30-5-50).

How does the value on the deed affect the fee?

The fee is set by the value of the realty, determined under 12-24-30, and counted in $500 units with any fraction rounding up. Here is how the statutory fee scales:

Stated value$500 unitsStatutory fee at $1.85
$100,000200$370
$200,000400$740
$350,000700$1,295

These figures are straight arithmetic from the per-$500 rate in 12-24-10. They leave out any separate filing charge the office sets.

What does recording look like for an estate or foreclosure deed?

Deeds that come out of an estate or a foreclosure follow the same recording steps, with different fee treatment. A deed in lieu of foreclosure, or a deed to the mortgagee under foreclosure proceedings, is on the exemption list (12-24-40(13)). A master-in-equity deed shifts liability for the fee to the grantee (12-24-20), which matters to a buyer at a foreclosure sale.

A deed of distribution from a personal representative is recorded like any other deed, and our probate page covers how that instrument works. For an estate deed, the register will still ask for an affidavit stating either the value or the exemption.

Why does an unrecorded deed cause trouble at a sale?

A buyer's title search reads the public record, and a deed that never reached the register does not appear there. Sellers who inherited a house or took title years ago sometimes find an older deed was signed but never recorded, which has to be fixed before a clean sale. The statute makes recording an orderly process, with deeds taken in the order lodged, so lodging the missing deed early starts that clock.

If you find a gap, call the register of deeds or the clerk of court in the county and ask what they need. A closing attorney can help sort it out.

More questions about South Carolina Recording a Deed

How much is the deed recording fee in South Carolina?

$1.85 per $500 of value or fraction, made up of $1.30 for the state and $0.55 for the county (12-24-10, 12-24-90). Other filing fees are set by the office.

Do I record at the courthouse or with the register of deeds?

It depends on the county. In counties not listed in 30-5-10(A), the clerk of court does the register's job.

How long does recording take?

The statute requires recording within thirty days of lodgment, in the order lodged (30-5-90).

Does a deed need witnesses in South Carolina?

Often yes. Acknowledgment before an officer is witnessed by two witnesses, but a subscribing witness affidavit is another route (30-5-30).

Do I need to record a deed at all?

Recording gives the public record the deed belongs in, and the statute sets the process once an instrument is lodged. Ask a closing attorney about priority questions.
